common_name: Prince of Wales Sweet Pea (Rose-Pink Grandiflora Heirloom, 1899)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight before sowing as soon as soil can be worked in early spring.

directions: This rose-pink grandiflora sweet pea dates to the late Victorian era and remains prized for its strong old-fashioned fragrance, a trait bred out of many modern Spencer types. Provide a trellis or netting at planting time since vines climb by tendril and resent late staking. Keep flowers picked continually to prevent seed set, which quickly halts bloom production. Deep, rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture through the cool part of the season produces the longest stems for cutting.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Mrs Bernard Jones Sweet Pea (Lavender-Blue Frilled Spencer)

planting.note: Fall-sow where winters stay mild, or start in root trainers in late winter for spring planting elsewhere.

directions: This exhibition-grade Spencer bears large, heavily waved lavender-blue standards over a lighter wing, a color combination that has kept it in show classes for decades. Pinch young plants once past the third node to encourage branching and a stronger root system before they begin to climb. Feed lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer once buds form, since excess nitrogen pushes foliage at the expense of flowers. Mulch to keep roots cool, as this cultivar is prone to stalling in early summer heat.
sources: National Sweet Pea Society (UK) cultivar records
Owen's Sweet Peas heirloom variety notes

common_name: Hungarian Blue Breadseed Poppy (Slate-Blue Seed Heirloom)

planting.note: Scatter seed on bare soil in very early spring or the prior fall, as the fine seed needs light and cold to germinate reliably.

directions: An old European farmhouse strain grown for both its lilac-mauve single flowers and its abundant slate-blue culinary seed, ready to harvest once the papery pods rattle and dry on the stem. Thin seedlings to their final spacing early, since breadseed poppies dislike root disturbance and rarely transplant well. Avoid rich, freshly manured soil, which tends to produce lush leaves and fewer pods. Leave a portion of pods to shatter for reliable self-sowing the following year.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds variety archive
Seed Savers Exchange Papaver somniferum notes

common_name: Falling in Love Poppy (Double Picotee Pink Shirley Poppy)

planting.note: Surface-sow directly outdoors in early spring, pressing seed lightly into soil without covering.

directions: This modern Shirley-type selection produces frilled, semi-double blooms edged in white with a rose-pink picotee margin, resembling crepe paper on wiry stems. Sow in successive small batches two weeks apart through early spring to extend the bloom window, since individual plants flower for only a few weeks. Deadhead spent blooms unless seed pods are wanted for winter arrangements. Choose a lean, well-drained site, as overly rich soil produces floppy stems that need staking.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds flower trial notes
Floret Flower Farm cut-flower poppy trials

planting.note: Direct-sow as soon as soil can be worked; nigella resents transplanting because of its fine taproot.

directions: A clean white-flowered selection of love-in-a-mist, valued by cut-flower growers for pairing with darker Nigella tones in mixed bouquets and for its ornamental, papery seed pods later in the season. Scatter seed thinly over prepared beds and rake in lightly, since the ferny foliage and flowers both look best when plants are allowed to grow close together in informal drifts. Succession sow every three weeks through late spring for a continuous cutting supply. Leave a few pods to dry on the plant for reliable self-sowing.
sources: Floret Flower Farm cut-flower Nigella notes

planting.note: Direct-sow in cool weather; a light fall sowing in mild climates gives earlier, stronger plants.

directions: This selection offers unusually deep wine-pink to mulberry-red flowers, a departure from the more common blue and white love-in-a-mist shades, set against the same finely dissected foliage. Grow in lean to average soil, since overly fertile ground encourages sprawling stems that flop before the inflated seed pods mature. Cut for fresh bouquets while flowers are just opening, or leave stems to develop their striped pods for dried arrangements. Thin seedlings to their final spacing while small, as roots are easily disturbed later.
sources: Sarah Raven cut-flower Nigella trial notes

planting.note: Chill seed in the refrigerator for one to two weeks before an early-spring or fall sowing to break dormancy.

directions: Blue Cloud produces dense spikes of soft sky-blue double florets on sturdy stems, a favorite among cut-flower growers for its cool, airy color in mixed bouquets. Sow where larkspur is to bloom, since the brittle taproot rarely survives transplanting once established. Support plants with corral netting early, as fully budded spikes can topple in wind and rain. Larkspur performs best where spring stays cool and fades quickly once summer heat arrives, so plan cutting for late spring.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds larkspur variety notes
Floret Flower Farm larkspur cut-flower trials

common_name: Cloudy Skies Larkspur (Smoky Lilac-Grey Double Larkspur)

planting.note: Fall-sow in mild-winter regions for the tallest spikes, or direct-sow in earliest spring while soil is still cold.

directions: A smoky lilac-grey companion to Earl Grey, this double-flowered larkspur is grown by specialty cut-flower farms for its muted, painterly color that blends easily with both pastel and jewel-toned bouquets. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil, since larkspur roots rot quickly in standing water during wet spring weather. Cut when the lower third of the spike has opened for the longest vase life. Remove spent flower spikes before pods fully mature unless collecting seed, since larkspur is quick to self-sow in favorable beds.
sources: Floret Flower Farm larkspur cut-flower trials
